name: Jōmon culture
info: The hunter-gatherer and early farming culture of the Japanese archipelago from c. 14,000 to 300 BCE, known for cord-marked pottery among the oldest in the world, settled villages and dogū figurines.

facts.homeland: The Japanese archipelago from Hokkaido to Kyushu, with most people in Honshu and Kyushu; the Jōmon were mostly absent from Okinawa and the Ryukyu Islands. Key sites: Odai Yamamoto I, Kamikuroiwa, the Fukui cave and the Ikawazu shell mound at Tahara.
facts.period: c. 14,000–300 BCE: Incipient 13,750–8,500 BCE, Initial 8,500–5,000, Early 5,000–3,520, Middle 3,520–2,470, Late 2,470–1,250 and Final 1,250–500 BCE, the end of the Final phase now refined to c. 300 BCE.
facts.known: cord-marked pottery among the oldest in the world; “flame style” vessels; dogū figurines; lacquerware; magatama curved stone beads; pit-houses; shell middens; tended groves of chestnut and lacquer trees; the early domestication of the adzuki bean
facts.sources: Excavated sites and shell middens; pottery typology (some 70 styles) and radiocarbon dating; skeletal and dental studies; ancient DNA and full-genome analyses; loanwords in Japanese. The Jōmon left no writing.

t: For some 14,000 years the people of the Japanese archipelago lived mainly by hunting, gathering and fishing, yet many settled in villages, reaching a considerable degree of sedentism and cultural complexity.
Jōmon potters made the world’s oldest known ceramics, around 14,500 BCE; their pottery was typically decorated by pressing cords into the wet clay, the pattern that gives the culture its name.
The Jōmon people later mixed with the Yayoi rice farmers: modern Japanese carry part of their ancestry, and two Jōmon populations of Hokkaido merged to form the proto-Ainu.
dyk: A domesticated peach, already similar to modern cultivated forms, appears at Jōmon sites around 4700–4400 BCE, earlier than a variety so close to modern peaches is attested in China itself.
ev: Jōmon hunter-gatherers make the world’s oldest known pottery, fragments of which survive at Odai Yamamoto I
As the glaciers melt at the end of the last glacial period, rising seas separate the archipelago from the Asian mainland
The Early Jōmon begins in the warm Holocene climatic optimum, with a rise in population and larger villages
A domesticated peach, apparently brought from China, appears at Jōmon sites
The Middle Jōmon, the warmest phase, produces “flame style” vessels, dogū figurines and more elaborate pit-houses
The climate cools and the population appears to contract dramatically
Korean-type settlements bringing wet rice farming and bronze and iron metallurgy are established in western Kyushu
Edward S. Morse finds cord-marked sherds and gives the culture its name

sections.origins:
The Jōmon period is the archaeologists’ name for the long stretch of Japanese prehistory between about 14,000 and 300 BCE, when the archipelago was home to a diverse population of hunter-gatherers and early cultivators who shared a common culture. Its earliest, Incipient phase began while Japan was still joined to continental Asia as a narrow peninsula. As the glaciers melted after the end of the last glacial period, around 12,000 BCE, rising seas cut the islands off from the mainland. Kyushu remained about 190 km from the Korean Peninsula, close enough for occasional continental influence but far enough for the islands to develop on their own.

Where the Jōmon people came from is studied through skeletons, teeth and DNA, and the answers differ. Full-genome analyses published in 2020 and 2021 suggest an early mixing of different groups in Japan during the Palaeolithic, followed by steady gene flow from coastal East Asia, producing a varied population that became more uniform before the Yayoi arrived. Part of this ancestry has been traced to a source population near the Himalayas, reaching Japan by an inland route through southern or central China; another component reached Hokkaido from Siberia. Other studies point to a single wave of migration, with regional differences explained by genetic drift, and others again to ancestors in Southeast Asia.

The name comes from the American zoologist Edward S. Morse, who found cord-marked sherds in 1877; his phrase “straw-rope pattern” was rendered in Japanese as Jōmon. The great age of the pottery was recognised only after the Second World War, through radiocarbon dating. The period is divided into six phases, Incipient, Initial, Early, Middle, Late and Final, dated mainly by the styles of pottery and to a lesser extent by radiocarbon dates. A single name for so long a period hides considerable differences between regions and over time.
sections.society:
The forests that spread after the Ice Age fed the Jōmon well. In the south-west broadleaf evergreen trees dominated; in north-eastern Honshu and southern Hokkaido, broadleaf deciduous trees and conifers. Beeches, buckeyes, chestnuts and oaks gave nuts and acorns that were stored for the winter in underground pits, especially in the east, though some acorns had to be processed to remove their bitter tannins before they could be eaten. In the north-east the Oyashio Current brought salmon and other sea life. People also ate sika deer, wild boar, freshwater fish and wild plants such as yam-like tubers, and coastal communities left great middens of discarded shells, now a major source for archaeologists. Most people lived in Honshu and Kyushu.

How far the Jōmon farmed is debated. There is evidence that they tended groves of chestnut and lacquer trees and grew soybean, bottle gourd, hemp, perilla and adzuki beans, which places them somewhere between hunting-gathering and agriculture. A genomic study traced all present-day adzuki cultivars to wild adzuki in eastern Japan, with the traits of domestication being selected from about 10,000 years ago.

The Early Jōmon, from about 5000 BCE, fell in the warm, humid Holocene climatic optimum and saw a sharp rise in population and larger villages. People lived in pit-houses, which grew more complex in the Middle Jōmon, some with paved stone floors; in the Late Jōmon the Japanese chestnut became the main building timber because it lasted well in wet conditions. After 1500 BCE the climate cooled and the population appears to have contracted dramatically. At the end of the period numbers fell sharply again, possibly through food shortages and other environmental problems; the skeletons show no warfare or violence on a scale that could explain the decline.
sections.beliefs:
The Jōmon left no writing, so their beliefs can only be inferred from what they made and how they treated their dead. Some of the clearest clues come from the Middle Jōmon, between about 3520 and 2470 BCE. In this phase magatama, curved stone beads, changed from a common ornament found in homes into grave goods placed with the dead. The same phase saw large burial mounds and monuments.

The Middle Jōmon also left highly ornate clay figurines, the dogū. The archaeologist Jun Takayama has argued that the patterns on dogū depict tattoos, which would make them a record of how the Jōmon marked their own bodies. That reading is a theory, not a settled fact.

Some elements of later Japanese culture, among them the precursors of Shinto, may reach back to this period, shaped by the meeting of the local Jōmon peoples with migrants from the northern Asian continent and the southern Pacific. Japan’s own founding stories also place their beginnings within what is now the Jōmon period: the traditional date for the founding of the nation by Emperor Jimmu is 11 February 660 BCE. These stories come from the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki, the country’s first written records, set down between the 6th and 8th centuries CE after Japan had adopted Chinese characters, and they show little or no relation to what archaeology has found of Jōmon culture.
sections.arts:
Jōmon potters made the world’s oldest known ceramics. Fragments dated to about 14,500 BCE were found at the Odai Yamamoto I site in 1998, and pottery of roughly the same age has since come from Kamikuroiwa and the Fukui cave. The earliest vessels were mostly small round-bottomed bowls 10–50 cm high, thought to have been used for boiling food and perhaps for storing it. Their small size may reflect the need to carry them, and the larger bowls of later times are taken as a sign of a more settled way of life. Pottery is heavy, bulky and fragile and unsuited to fully nomadic people, which suggests that the islands’ abundant food could support fairly large, semi-sedentary populations.

The typical decoration was made by pressing cords into the wet clay. Over time vessels gained more elaborate patterns, undulating rims and flat bottoms so that they could stand on a level surface. Archaeologists classify Jōmon pottery into some 70 styles, with many more local varieties, from the linear appliqué and nail-impressed wares of the Incipient phase to the Kamegaoka and other styles of the Final phase. The Middle Jōmon produced the most ornate pieces, including the “flame style” vessels and dogū figurines, though the clay itself always remained quite coarse.

Beyond pottery, the Jōmon made tools and jewellery of bone, stone, shell and antler, chipped and ground stone tools, traps and bows, and lacquered wooden objects. They were skilful coastal and deep-water fishers. Lacquerware and the laminated bow called the yumi are among the technologies that may have passed from this period into later Japanese culture.
sections.exchange:
Japan’s position gave the Jōmon several routes of contact: through the Korean Peninsula to Kyushu and Honshu, along the island chain of Luzon, Taiwan and the Ryukyus to Southeast Asia, and through Hokkaido and Sakhalin to Siberia. A domesticated peach appears at Jōmon sites around 4700–4400 BCE and was apparently brought from China. Archaeological and biological evidence links the southern Jōmon of Kyushu, Shikoku and parts of Honshu with southern China and north-eastern India, within a shared “broadleafed evergreen forest culture” marked by the growing of adzuki beans. Genetic studies have also detected gene flow from ancient Siberia into the northern Jōmon of Hokkaido.

Language is harder to trace. Some linguists argue that Austronesian-speaking peoples reached Japan during the Jōmon period, pointing to Austronesian words in the core vocabulary of Japanese, while genome studies have found no Austronesian-related ancestry in the Jōmon, including those of the Ryukyus. Japanese also holds loanwords that are neither Ainu, Austronesian nor Korean and probably come from unknown, extinct Jōmon languages. Some linguists suggest that the Japonic languages were already spoken by one of the Jōmon populations of south-western Japan before the Yayoi period.

In the Final Jōmon, contact with the Korean Peninsula grew steadily, and from around 900 BCE Korean-type settlements were founded in western Kyushu. Their settlers brought wet rice farming, bronze and iron metallurgy and pottery like that of the Mumun pottery period, and their villages seem to have existed alongside those of the Jōmon and Yayoi for around a thousand years. Further afield, Jōmon society is often compared with the Valdivia culture of Ecuador and the peoples of the North American Pacific Northwest, where cultural complexity also grew from hunting and gathering; whether their likenesses arose independently or through Jōmon seafarers who lost their way is debated.
sections.legacy:
The Jōmon period ended at different times and in different ways across the archipelago. Outside Hokkaido it gave way to the Yayoi, a farming culture of about 300 BCE to 300 CE named after an archaeological site near Tokyo; radiocarbon evidence places the start of the Yayoi between 500 and 300 BCE, while Yayoi-style pottery has been found at a Jōmon site in northern Kyushu dated to 800 BCE. In Hokkaido and northern Tōhoku the Jōmon were followed instead by the related Zoku-Jōmon, or Epi-Jōmon, culture and by the Okhotsk culture, which later merged with or were replaced by the Satsumon culture around the 7th century CE. In Okinawa and the Ryukyus, where Jōmon people were mostly absent, archaeologists use a chronology of their own, the Shellmidden Period.

The Jōmon people mixed with the Yayoi, and modern Japanese carry part of their ancestry: about 30% on the paternal side, about 15% on the maternal side and about 10% across the whole genome. This imbalance, called the “admixture paradox”, is thought to hold clues to how the two populations mixed. In Hokkaido, two distinct Jōmon populations later merged to form the proto-Ainu.

Public views of the Jōmon have changed from seeing them as primitive to finding them captivating. Since the 1970s potters have revived ancient Jōmon techniques such as firing in a bonfire, and in the early 21st century cord-marking returned on clothing, accessories and tattoos. Jōmon motifs appear on vessels, origami, sweets, notebooks and neckties, Jōmon-style pit houses have been rebuilt at places such as the Jōmon Village Historic Garden, and in 2018 a Jōmon exhibition at the Tokyo National Museum drew 350,000 visitors, three and a half times the number expected.

summary: The Jōmon culture flourished in the Japanese archipelago from about 14,000 to 300 BCE, a long era of hunter-gatherers and early cultivators who lived in increasingly settled villages. Its potters made the world’s oldest known ceramics and the cord-marked wares that give it its name, as well as dogū figurines and lacquerware. Its people later mixed with rice farmers from the continent and are among the ancestors of the Japanese and the Ainu.

notes: Dates kept at -14000/-300. The article gives the Final phase as 1,250–500 BCE but says recent findings refine the end to 300 BCE; it also says the Yayoi began between 500 and 300 BCE by radiocarbon, with Yayoi-style pottery at a northern Kyushu Jōmon site in 800 BCE. The Incipient phase dates differ inside the article (13,750–8,500 BC in the chronology, 14,000–7500 BCE in the ceramic typology); facts.period uses the chronology section.

The origin section of the article is internally contradictory (ancestors from Southeast Asia; single-wave migration; Himalayan/inland China source; Austronesian presence by linguistics vs no Austronesian input by genomes). I presented them as differing views rather than choosing.
The article’s References section was not saved; the five references are from its Further reading list (Habu 2001’s publisher is given there as Berghahn Books, as written).

Beliefs section is short (about 1,400 characters): the article says little about Jōmon religion beyond magatama as grave goods, burial mounds, dogū and Takayama’s tattoo theory. I did not add interpretations of dogū or ‘flame style’ pots that the article does not give.

No UNESCO listing or museum other than the 2018 Tokyo National Museum exhibition and the Jōmon Village Historic Garden is named in the article (the Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan World Heritage listing is not in it, so it is left out).
The Ainu are mentioned only as descendants (proto-Ainu from Hokkaido Jōmon); the article does not cover the Ainu’s later history, so the profile does not either.
